title: APT38
summary: APT38, tracked by vendors as Bluenoroff, Stardust Chollima and Sapphire Sleet, is a financially motivated cluster that public reporting links to the North Korean government and treats as a sibling of the Lazarus Group. Reporting from the United States Government and private vendors describes intrusions against banks and payment networks across Asia, Africa and the Americas, with techniques that avoid damaging the victim's own systems because the goal is to move money rather than to disrupt operations. The tradecraft reported includes custom remote access tools, credential theft, careful study of internal payment procedures, and manipulation of the messages that banks exchange when transferring funds, including steps taken to hide evidence of the fraudulent transfers. Attribution rests on overlapping infrastructure and shared tooling with other tracked clusters and is stated by governments as an assessment, so defenders should treat shared indicators as one input among many rather than as proof of a single actor.

beginner.definition: APT38 is a group that steals money from banks using computers. Public reports link it to the government of North Korea and to the Lazarus Group. The name Bluenoroff is also used for the same activity. Their goal is cash, not damage, so they try to keep bank systems running normally. Different security companies use different names, which makes the reporting hard to compare.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group studies how a bank moves money and then copies the process. That means the weakest point is often a human procedure, not a piece of software. If staff can approve large transfers alone, or if test systems hold real data, the risk is high. Only a few teams review who approves what, and that review is cheap. It also shows that peace time and crisis time call for the same controls.
howItWorks: The attackers get a first foothold through a fake email or a weak public service.
They quietly collect usernames and passwords from every system they manage to reach.
They study how the bank approves and sends large payments to other banks.
They create or reuse accounts that look exactly like the accounts of normal staff.
They then send fraudulent payment messages to other banks on behalf of the victim.
They remove or alter records so that the transfers look completely ordinary afterwards.
beginner.example: Imagine a mail room where clerks send money orders with a stamped form. A thief studies the form, copies the stamp, and sends orders that look perfect to the receiving office. The receiving office pays, because the paper looks right. The thief never breaks a window; he learns your forms and your routines, then copies them exactly.
takeaways: Attackers often copy your procedures instead of breaking your software.
Make sure no single person can approve a large payment alone.
Attribution to a country is a judgement, so base your defence on behaviour.

objectives: Explain why financially motivated intrusions may avoid damaging victim systems.
Describe how payment approval procedures become an attack target.
Explain the meaning of attribution and why confidence levels matter.
List controls that reduce the risk of fraudulent fund transfers.
Explain why shared indicators alone do not prove who is behind an intrusion.
